title: Choose the number of options on purpose
statement: Choose how many options a question offers on purpose: avoid two-option items, cap how many a young reader must weigh, and never add a filler option to reach a count.
example: One item offered an eight-year-old twelve selectable options.
detail: A review of the Grade 3 course asked for at least four options on multiple-choice questions, because a two-option yes-or-no item permits a 50/50 guess (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0136-g3-reading-v2-reviewer-feedback.qmd`). An earlier review found a hot-text item with twelve selectable options, too heavy a motor and cognitive load for an eight-year-old, and asked for the number to be capped (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0081-g3-reviewer-feedback-raw-2026-07-02-reading-explorers-v2-review-verbatim.qmd`). The project's routing note says an agent must not settle the question of three or four options by adding filler (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`), and later course feedback agrees that the four-option request is not a license for a weak fourth distractor (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0172-g3-reading-course-feedback-2026-08-04.qmd`). Two-option and yes/no items let a guess get them right half the time. Offer only as many options as can be made plausible.
against: the multiple-choice BrainLift the project follows reports a research consensus favouring three options and recommends four only when every distractor stays plausible and diagnostically useful, so the default count is still open (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`, lines 102-104). The reading course standardised on exactly four options to prevent guessing (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0183-copy-question-quality-rulings.qmd`), and its v2 review asked for at least four (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0136-g3-reading-v2-reviewer-feedback.qmd`), which leaves filler or a broken rule wherever a fourth plausible option can't be written. The sources split on the default: one rule fixes exactly four options and a review asks for at least four, while the multiple-choice BrainLift favours three and leaves the default to an explicit decision. The cap of five is a chosen limit; the scan counted items over it rather than measuring an effect on students. A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/extras/alpharead-lesson-design-aladdin-part-1.md`).
